{{Short description|English cleric and academic}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
'''James Devereux Hustler''' (1784–1849) was an English cleric and academic. He was a mathematician, elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 1819.<ref name="acad">{{acad|id=HSTR801JD|name=Hustler, James Devereux}}</ref>

==Early life==
He was the son of Thomas and Ann Hustler of [[Bury St Edmunds]]; his father (died 1800) was a grocer in Abbeygate Street.<ref name="acad"/><ref>{{cite book |title=The Oakes Diaries: Business, Politics and the Family in Bury St Edmunds 1778–1827 |volume=I|page=178 note 66 |url=https://suffolkrecordssociety.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/The-Oakes-Diaries-I.pdf |publisher=Boydell Press|editor=Jane Fiske|isbn=0851152759|date=1990}}</ref> William Hustler (died 1832), registrar of the [[University of Cambridge]], and Robert Samuel Hustler (died 1835) of the [[Royal Engineers]], who served at the [[Battle of Waterloo]] as a captain, were his brothers.<ref name="GM">{{cite book |title=The Gentleman's Magazine |date=1850 |publisher=E. Cave |page=103 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3gIOKVJxoYkC&pg=PA103 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Bromley |first1=Janet |last2=Bromley |first2=David |title=Wellington's Men Remembered Volume 2: A Register of Memorials to Soldiers who Fought in the Peninsular War and at Waterloo- Volume II: M to Z |date=25 March 2015 |publisher=Pen and Sword |isbn=978-1-84884-750-7 |page=605 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=n0euCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA605 |language=en}}</ref> He was educated at the [[King Edward VI Free School, Bury St Edmunds]], under the Rev. Michael Becher.<ref name="acad"/><ref>{{cite book |title=Biographical list of boys educated at King Edward VI. Free Grammar School, Bury St. Edmunds : From 1550 to 1900 ... |date=1908 |publisher=Bury St. Edmunds : Paul & Mathew |pages=202 |url=https://archive.org/details/b28994140/page/202/mode/1up}}</ref> [[Charles James Blomfield|Charles Blomfield]], who shared his background and education, and became [[Bishop of London]], was a good friend.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gurney |first1=Dorothy Frances Blomfield |title=The childhood of Queen Victoria |date=1901 |publisher=London : J. Nisbet |page=208 |url=https://archive.org/details/childhoodofqueen00gurniala/page/208/mode/1up}}</ref>

Hustler matriculated at [[Christ's College, Cambridge]] in 1801, moving to [[Trinity College, Cambridge|Trinity College]] in 1802. He was third [[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|Wrangler]] in 1806, after [[Sir Frederick Pollock, 1st Baronet|Frederick Pollock]] and [[Henry Walter (antiquary)|Henry Walter]], graduating B.A. He became a Fellow of Trinity in 1807.<ref name="acad"/><ref>{{cite book |last1=University of Cambridge |title=Historical Register of the University of Cambridge ... to the Year 1910 |date=1917 |page=300 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JSFFAQAAMAAJ |language=en}}</ref> That year, a five-hour interview between [[Thomas Smart Hughes]], then an undergraduate, and an increasingly drunken [[Richard Porson]], a close friend of Hustler's, took place in Hustler's college rooms.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Watson |first1=John Selby |title=The Life of Richard Porson, M. A.: Professor of Greek in the University of Cambridge from 1792 to 1808 |date=1861 |publisher=Longman, Green, Longman, and Roberts |pages=385–387 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CXcKAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA385 |language=en}}</ref>

In 1809 Hustler graduated M.A., and he graduated B.D. in 1816.<ref name="acad"/> [[Henry Gage, 4th Viscount Gage]] entered Trinity College in 1811, and graduated M.A. in 1812; he went on to write some mathematical works.<ref>{{acad|id=GG811HH|name=Gage, Henry Hall, Viscount.}}</ref> Hustler was appointed his domestic chaplain in 1813.<ref>{{CCEd |type=person |id=112720 |name=Hustler, James Devereux |year1=1808 |year2=1829 |accessed=8 November 2021 }}</ref> In 1813, also, Hustler became tutor to [[Spencer Perceval (junior)|Spencer Perceval the younger]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Trinity College, Cambridge |title=Admissions to Trinity College, Cambridge|date=1911 |publisher=Macmillan & Co., Ltd |page=95|volume=IV |language=en}}</ref>

==Trinity tutor==
Hustler was an assistant tutor at Trinity 1811–1813, and then tutor 1813–1823.<ref>{{cite web |title=Admissions to Trinity College, Cambridge|editor=W. W. Rouse Ball and J. A. Venn|volume=IV 1801 to 1850|page=9|publisher=Macmillan & Co.|location=London|url=https://brittlebooks.library.illinois.edu/brittlebooks_open/Books2009-06/trinco0001admtri/trinco0001admtriv00004/trinco0001admtriv00004.pdf}}</ref> His period as a tutor overlapped with the years 1815–1825 that have been dubbed the "analytical revolution" at Cambridge. In the teaching and examining of the [[infinitesimal calculus]], the notations and ideas of [[Gottfried Leibniz]] were introduced, alongside those traditionally taught of [[Isaac Newton]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Warwick |first1=Andrew |title=Masters of Theory: Cambridge and the Rise of Mathematical Physics |date=15 April 2011 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |isbn=978-0-226-87376-3 |page=69 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6vs8EAAAQBAJ&pg=PA69 |language=en}}</ref>

As a tutor, Hustler diverted [[George Airy]] away from applying to [[Peterhouse]], which had been recommended by [[Thomas Clarkson]], a friend of Hustler's, and taught him at Trinity.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Airy |first1=George Biddell |title=Autobiography of Sir George Biddell Airy |date=25 September 2019 |publisher=BoD – Books on Demand |isbn=978-3-7340-6678-8 |page=22 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BraxDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA22 |language=en}}</ref> Airy had been taught by a master at his school in [[Colchester]], Thomas Rogers (1789–1860), a graduate from [[Sidney Sussex College]] in 1811, covering the university topics to [[fluxion]]s and the ''Principia''. Hustler and his tutorial assistant [[George Peacock (mathematician)|George Peacock]] were in 1819 passed work by Airy.<ref name="SS">{{cite book |last1=Smith |first1=Jonathan |last2=Stray |first2=Christopher |title=Teaching and Learning in Nineteenth-century Cambridge |date=2001 |publisher=Boydell & Brewer |isbn=978-0-85115-783-2 |pages=20–22 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=P0X7F4mLTpkC&pg=PA20 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{acad|id=RGRS805T|name=Rogers, Thomas}}</ref> In 1820, Hustler arranged an [[exhibition (scholarship)|exhibition]] (minor scholarship) for Airy, via the Norwich Member of Parliament [[William Smith (abolitionist)|William Smith]].<ref name="Airy">{{cite book |last1=Airy |first1=George Biddell |title=Autobiography of Sir George Biddell Airy |date=25 September 2019 |publisher=BoD – Books on Demand |isbn=978-3-7340-6679-5 |pages=24–25 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=86mxDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA24 |language=en}}</ref>

Peacock then gave Airy special teaching in the contemporary calculus methods, and Airy responded by working over results of [[Samuel Vince]] and [[Robert Woodhouse]].<ref name="SS"/> When Airy began experimenting with the [[Argand diagram]] in 1820, Peacock encouraged him in linking it to [[trigonometry]], but Hustler disapproved.<ref name="Airy"/>

In 1822, Hustler intervened to place Airy and some of his peers, ahead of the usual schedule, in the "questionist" group of those being prepared for the final stage of the [[Mathematical Tripos]]. There was resistance from the more senior students. The accelerated group was then taught separately, by Peacock.<ref name="SS"/>

==Later life==
Hustler's clerical career began in 1823, when he was a curate at [[Fornham All Saints]].<ref name="acad"/> In 1828 the [[George Henry FitzRoy, 4th Duke of Grafton|Duke of Grafton]] presented him to the rectory of [[Great Fakenham]], and in 1829 to the living of [[Euston, Suffolk]].<ref name="GM"/><ref name="Proceedings">{{cite book |last1=History |first1=Suffolk Institute of Archaeology and Natural |title=Proceedings |date=1894 |page=305 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k0YJAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA305 |language=en}}</ref>

As a benefactor, Hustler gave a [[paten]] to Fornham All Saints, and an organ to St John's Church, Bury St Edmunds, built 1840–1.<ref name="Proceedings"/><ref>{{cite book |last1=White |first1=William |title=History, gazetteer, and directory, of Suffolk |date=1855 |page=179 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KO8NAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA179 |language=en}}</ref>

==Works==
* ''The Elements of Conic Sections: with the sections of conoids'' (1st edition 1818, 2nd edition 1820, 3rd edition 1826), anonymous.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hustler |first1=James Devereux |title=The Elements of the Conic Sections with the Sections of the Conoids |date=1820 |publisher=J. Smith |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3bAdkyc5K4kC |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Cushing |first1=William |title=Anonyms: A Dictionary of Revealed Authorship |date=1889 |publisher=W. Cushing |isbn=978-3-487-02714-2 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uguppL6eUO4C&pg=PA201 |language=en}}</ref> A revised edition of 1845 was published under Hustler's name.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Errata |journal=The Mathematical Gazette |date=1927 |volume=13 |issue=186 |page=292 |doi=10.1017/S0025557200109726 |jstor=3602051 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3602051 |issn=0025-5572|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* ''A Sermon preached [...] the first Sunday after the funeral of [...] George Henry Duke of Grafton'' (1844)<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hustler |first1=James Devereux |title=A Sermon preached ... the first Sunday after the funeral of ... George Henry Duke of Grafton |date=1844 |publisher=W. T. Jackson |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=m7-UwoN4RhgC |language=en}}</ref>
* ''Unity in the Church: A Sermon Preached at Ixworth on Monday, May 21st, 1849'' (1849)<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hustler |first1=James Devereux |title=Unity in the Church: A Sermon Preached at Ixworth on Monday, May 21st, 1849 at the Annual Visitation of the Ven. Archdeacon Glover |date=1849 |publisher=W.T. Jackson |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gFFxuAAACAAJ |language=en}}</ref>

==Family==
Hustler married Elizabeth Mansel, daughter of [[William Lort Mansel]], in 1823.<ref>{{cite news |title=Married |url=https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0001669/18230222/035/0003 |work=Norwich Mercury|page=3 |date=22 February 1823}}</ref> Of their children:

* James Devereux Hustler, the eldest son, married in 1852 Isabella Carruthers, eldest daughter of George Edwardes Carruthers, a surgeon, and Anne Smith, daughter of [[Sir David William Smith, 1st Baronet]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Marriages |url=https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000183/18520527/038/0004 |work=London Evening Standard |date=27 May 1852|page=4}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=The Spectator |date=1844 |publisher=F.C. Westley |pages=851 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=O9M9AQAAIAAJ&pg=PA851 |language=en}}</ref>
* Spencer William Hustler, married in 1854 Anne Leach, eldest daughter of the Rev. Francis George Leach of Stackpole.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cave |first1=Edward |title=Gentleman's Magazine, Or Monthly Intelligencer |date=1854 |publisher=Edward Cave |page=522 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9PRfAAAAcAAJ&pg=PA522 |language=en}}</ref>
* Elizabeth Juliana, married in 1855 James Robertson Bryant of Pembroke as his second wife.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Nicholas |first1=Thomas |title=Annals and Antiquities of the Counties and County Families of Wales: Containing a Record of All Ranks of the Gentry ... with Many Ancient Pedigrees and Memorials of Old and Extinct Families |date=1872 |publisher=Longmans, Green, Reader |page=896 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qjIwAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA896 |language=en}}</ref>
* Augusta Frederica, the youngest daughter, married in 1856 the Rev. Owen Jones.<ref>{{cite book |title=The Ecclesiastical gazette, or, Monthly register of the affairs of the Church of England |date=1857 |page=13 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ap0OAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA13 |language=en}}</ref> In 1888 their daughter Elizabeth Frederica Isabella Owen married the Rev. William Howard Coates, son of William Henry Coates and his wife [[Elizabeth Youatt]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Marriage of the Rev. W. H. Coates |url=https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0001981/18880915/038/0003 |work=Hampstead & Highgate Express |date=15 September 1888|page=3}}</ref>

Portraits of their children were painted in 1833 by [[Samuel Lane (painter)|Samuel Lane]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Graves |first1=Algernon |title=The Royal Academy of Arts; a complete dictionary of contributors and their work from its foundation in 1769 to 1904 |date=1972 |publisher=New York, B. Franklin |page=389|volume=IV |url=https://archive.org/details/royalacademyart05gravgoog/page/n389/mode/1up}}</ref>
